blocks.text: Ruth 2 moves Naomi and Ruth from bereavement into the setting of harvest. Ruth goes to glean, reaches the field of Boaz, and receives protection, water, food, and additional grain from him. Boaz has heard of Ruth's loyalty to Naomi and blesses her refuge under the God of Israel. When Ruth returns with an abundant amount of barley, Naomi learns that Boaz is a near relative and recognizes a new possibility for the living and the dead.

sections.title: Gleaning and protection in the harvest

blocks.text: In this chapter, gleaning is survival labor. Boaz's response goes beyond allowing Ruth to collect leftover grain: he directs her to stay with his workers, orders the young men not to touch her, provides access to water and food, and tells the reapers to pull grain from the bundles for her. The contrast shows that protection and provision are part of the help Ruth receives, not merely permission to enter a field.

Ruth's story is set in the judges-era world of harvest labor, kinship obligations, land continuity, and public negotiation. That setting helps explain why Naomi pays close attention to the identity of the landowner: Boaz is not just a successful farmer in the story, but a near relative whose household and property are connected to Naomi's family.

The chapter explicitly speaks of the LORD while the plot advances through the actions of Ruth, Naomi, Boaz, the workers, and the women of Bethlehem. Ruth's food and safety come through concrete human decisions, so the chapter's account of divine care is narrated through harvest work, hospitality, protection, and kinship rather than detached from them.

sections.title: From emptiness to harvest and redemption

blocks.text: Ruth moves from famine, bereavement, and Naomi's emptiness toward harvest, kinship redemption, birth, communal blessing, and genealogy. Chapter 2 is the turning point where the harvest supplies immediate food and Boaz's kinship opens the larger path that the rest of the book will develop.
